summary.text: Job of Pochaev is remembered as an abbot, ascetic, and defender of Orthodox communities after the Union of Brest. His life combines solitary prayer with building, publishing, and practical care for the monastery.

blocks.text: Born Ivan Zhelezo in Galicia, he enters the Ugornits monastery as a child and receives tonsure with the name Job. Prince Constantine Ostrozhsky later asks him to lead the Holy Cross monastery near Dubno.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: The ACROD account places his formation within Orthodox family life and a monastery entered at ten. It follows his early tonsure, priestly ordination, and two decades of leadership at Dubno. The regional setting includes pressure on Orthodox institutions and a struggle to sustain instruction and worship.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: At Pochaev he is elected abbot and works with the brethren in gardens and waterworks. The OCA links his defense of Orthodoxy with copying and distributing books and notes his presence at the Kiev council of 1628.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: The diocesan article describes a cave used for withdrawal and prayer beside the demands of common life. It also follows disputes over the monastery’s property and the dangers faced by the brotherhood. Miraculous light in the cave is attributed to the life and its named disciple-witness, rather than independently demonstrated here.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: The OCA dates his repose to 1651 after more than fifty years directing Pochaev. It does not say he was killed. It records the uncovering of his relics in 1659 and again in 1833.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: The diocesan narrative gives October 28 for his repose after the Liturgy and says he dies peacefully. Its extraordinary lifespan and foreknowledge of death remain elements of the hagiographical account.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: Both accounts remember the defense of Orthodox teaching through books and pastoral work. The diocesan article places Pochaev within the memory of several neighboring peoples; its polemical reading of regional church conflict remains an identified Orthodox interpretation. It should not be mistaken for the beliefs of every contemporary Catholic or Protestant.

blocks.title: Scripture on humility in prayer — Luke 18:9–14
blocks.text:
And he spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others:

Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican.

The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.

I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.

And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.

I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
